precepts.text: Our soul loatheth this light bread; the murmuring shows the false comfort Israel took in Egypt.
precepts.point: So God led the people about, through the way of the wilderness of the Red Sea, and the children of Israel went up harnessed out of the land of Egypt.

note.label: Exodus 13: By Strength of Hand the Lord Brought Us Out

precepts.why:
“And the people spake against God, and against Moses, Wherefore have ye brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? for there is no bread, neither is there any water; and our soul loatheth this light bread.” The Lord fed them from heaven, and they loathed it, and asked why they were ever brought up out of Egypt.

That murmuring shows the false comfort Israel took in Egypt. At the first hardship they looked back. That is exactly why God said “Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt” and led them the long way: a people who loathe the light bread and miss Egypt for its food would have turned back at the first sight of the Philistines.

The same spirit is in the people in America today, holding on to a little job, government assistance, a car and food from the store, never wanting this kingdom to come down.

precepts.text: Nicodemus, a Pharisee, a ruler of the Jews, came to Christ by night; an Israelite came to an Israelite.
precepts.point: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness to save Israel from death, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: the same way Israel beheld the serpent and did not perish, whosoever believes on Christ shall not perish but have eternal life. And the whosoever is defined in Acts: whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved; ye men of Israel, hear these words. The salvation spoken of is for Israel.

note.label: Numbers 21: The Fiery Serpents and the Serpent of Brass

precepts.why:
Christ brought the serpent of brass to Nicodemus. “There was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews: The same came to Jesus by night, and said unto him, Rabbi, we know that thou art a teacher come from God: for no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except God be with him.”

Nicodemus was a Pharisee, a ruler of the Jews, and he came to Christ, who is also a Jew: an Israelite came to an Israelite. Two Israelites speaking together about the history of Israel, the fiery serpents that bit the people and the serpent of brass on the pole.

precepts.text: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish.
precepts.point: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness to save Israel from death, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: the same way Israel beheld the serpent and did not perish, whosoever believes on Christ shall not perish but have eternal life. And the whosoever is defined in Acts: whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved; ye men of Israel, hear these words. The salvation spoken of is for Israel.

note.label: Numbers 21: The Fiery Serpents and the Serpent of Brass

precepts.why:
Moses “made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.” Read it with the nation in view: the people being bitten, the people dying, all of it is Israel. That brass serpent was for the Israelites, to heal the Israelites, because it was the Israelites being bitten for rebelling against God and against Moses. The symbol on ambulances today, a snake wrapped around a pole, comes from this scripture.

Christ told Nicodemus, “And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.”

As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness to save Israel from death, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: the same way Israel beheld the serpent and did not perish, whosoever believes on Christ shall not perish but have eternal life. The serpent healed Israel; the Son of man lifted up saves Israel.

precepts.text: Whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved; ye men of Israel, hear these words. The whosoever is spoken to Israel.
precepts.point: As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness to save Israel from death, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: the same way Israel beheld the serpent and did not perish, whosoever believes on Christ shall not perish but have eternal life. And the whosoever is defined in Acts: whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved; ye men of Israel, hear these words. The salvation spoken of is for Israel.

note.label: Numbers 21: The Fiery Serpents and the Serpent of Brass

precepts.why:
Christ said “whosoever believeth in him should not perish”, and the whosoever is defined in Acts. “And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved. Ye men of Israel, hear these words; Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved of God among you by miracles and wonders and signs, which God did by him in the midst of you, as ye yourselves also know.”

Whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved, and the next words are, ye men of Israel, hear these words. The whosoever is spoken to Israel.

The serpent of brass was lifted up for the Israelites that were bitten, and the salvation spoken of in the Son of man lifted up is for Israel.

precepts.text: The fiery serpents of the wilderness: the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people, and much people of Israel died.
precepts.point: He led thee through that great and terrible wilderness, wherein were fiery serpents and scorpions and drought, brought thee water out of the rock of flint, and fed thee with manna, to humble thee and to prove thee, to do thee good at thy latter end.

note.label: Deuteronomy 8: Keep the Commandments and Live

precepts.why:
“And the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died.” These are the fiery serpents of the wilderness.

Moses reminds Israel who led them “through that great and terrible wilderness, wherein were fiery serpents, and scorpions, and drought, where there was no water”. The serpents were real, sent by the Lord, and much people of Israel died of them. Yet he brought forth water out of the rock of flint and fed them with manna, to humble them and to prove them, “to do thee good at thy latter end”.

precepts.text: The destruction of Sihon and Og on the other side Jordan was the report that reached Jericho.
precepts.point: Her faith came by report: we have heard how the Lord dried up the water of the Red Sea for you, and what ye did unto Sihon and Og, the two kings of the Amorites whom ye utterly destroyed; and as soon as we had heard it, our hearts did melt, neither did there remain any more courage in any man. The Lord had said he would put that spirit on the nations.

note.label: Joshua 2: Rahab and the Spies

precepts.why:
Rahab's faith came by report: “we have heard how the Lord dried up the water of the Red sea for you, when ye came out of Egypt; and what ye did unto the two kings of the Amorites, that were on the other side Jordan, Sihon and Og, whom ye utterly destroyed.” This is what she heard. “And the Lord said unto Moses, Fear him not: for I have delivered him into thy hand, and all his people, and his land; and thou shalt do to him as thou didst unto Sihon king of the Amorites, which dwelt at Heshbon. So they smote him, and his sons, and all his people, until there was none left him alive: and they possessed his land.”

The destruction of Sihon and Og on the other side Jordan, none left alive, was the report that reached Jericho. When Rahab heard it, she knew the Lord is not to be played with when it comes to this people.

precepts.text: Woe to thee, Moab; thou art undone, O people of Chemosh. Chemosh was the god Moab was serving.
precepts.point: Naomi said, Thy sister in law is gone back unto her people and unto her gods. Those gods were idols; Chemosh was the god the Moabites served.

note.label: Ruth 1: Naomi and Ruth Return from Moab

precepts.why:
“Woe to thee, Moab! thou art undone, O people of Chemosh: he hath given his sons that escaped, and his daughters, into captivity unto Sihon king of the Amorites.”

Moab is called the people of Chemosh. Chemosh was the god the Moabites served, the idol Orpah went back to.

precepts.text: Much people of Israel died, and every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.
precepts.point: The serpent of brass was a sign of salvation, and it came with remembrance of the commandment of the law. Looking on it was not the whole of it; there was repentance with it.

note.label: John 3: Nicodemus, the Serpent Lifted Up, and Who the World Is

precepts.why:
“as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up”. The history behind that is plain, and so is who it was for. “And the people spake against God, and against Moses, Wherefore have ye brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? for there is no bread, neither is there any water; and our soul loatheth this light bread.”

“And the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died.” It was Israel in the wilderness that spake against the Most High and against Moses, and Israel that was bitten. “Therefore the people came to Moses, and said, We have sinned, for we have spoken against the Lord, and against thee; pray unto the Lord, that he take away the serpents from us. And Moses prayed for the people.”

“And the Lord said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live. And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.” It was Israel that looked and lived. Even so the Son of man was lifted up, “That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life”: the same people, bitten, looking, and living.

moments.label: The Book of the Wars of the Lord

points: This is where the topic comes from: wherefore it is said in the book of the wars of the Lord, what he did in the Red Sea, and in the brooks of Arnon. What he did in the Red Sea is in Exodus.

The question is this: the book of the wars of the Lord, where is it? Do we have that book? There is a book called the book of the wars of the Lord, a book that went into the wars of the Lord, and we do not have it. But reading the other scriptures, we are able to piece certain things together.

And when it says the wars of the Lord, who is the Lord there? It is talking about Christ. You think Christ is just going to come in the future and war? No. He has been warring ever since the beginning, ever since Exodus.

Counted in class: a traditional 80 book Protestant Bible consists of 39 Old Testament books, 27 New Testament books, and 14 Apocrypha books. Eighty books in all. Keep that in mind, because we just read about a book of the wars of the Lord, and that book is not in the Bible.

note.label: Numbers 21: The Fiery Serpents and the Serpent of Brass

points: The Canaanites are identified in this teaching with the people called Africans today. The place was called Hormah, which means utter destruction, because that is exactly what Israel did to them there.

No other nation on this earth takes food as seriously as Israel; even the complaints over bread and water are a familiar mark of this people to this day. You cannot put another nation in these scriptures.
